prompt: A team needs an index for extremely high write volume where keys arrive in random order. Structurally, which is the better fit and why?
choices: A B-tree, because B-trees always guarantee O(log n) worst-case time regardless of insertion order
An LSM-tree, because writes always land in an append-only memtable/log regardless of key order, while a B-tree's page-fill efficiency and write cost depend on the order keys arrive in
Neither — a plain hash table always outperforms both for high write volume
A B-tree, because LSM-trees require every read to scan the entire dataset

prompt: What three-letter acronym names the conjecture stating that a data access method can be optimized for at most two of Read performance, Update performance, and Memory/space overhead, but not all three simultaneously?
Redis implements its sorted-set type as a skip list rather than a balanced tree. Which architectural consequence follows most directly from that specific choice?
choices: Sorted sets require a dedicated background compaction thread to stay balanced

Ordered range queries (ZRANGE / ZRANGEBYSCORE) can be served by a simple forward pointer-chase at the bottom level, with none of the parent-pointer or explicit-stack bookkeeping a tree-based in-order traversal needs
Skip lists guarantee strictly better worst-case complexity than any balanced tree, which is the only reason Redis chose one
Skip lists remove the need for atomic single-command updates, since Redis runs commands across many threads at once
